pedagogy.summary:
• Age/Topic — 6–7: count to 120 starting at ANY number below 120, and read/write numerals to 120 — pushing counting and numeral fluency just past the 100 boundary into early three-digit territory.
• Standards — UK (DfE NC Mathematics, Y1–Y2): 'count to and across 100, forwards and backwards, beginning with 0 or 1, or from any given number' (Y1); the to-120 extension mirrors the US Grade 1 expectation.
• Standards — US (CCSS-M): 1.NBT.1 'count to 120, starting at any number less than 120; read and write numerals and represent a number of objects with a written numeral'.
• Operational details — two things matter: (i) counting on from any starting number (not always from 1), which shows counting is a movable sequence, and (ii) crossing 100 — reading/writing 100–120 (one hundred and eight = 108), where the hundreds place appears and children must not write 'one hundred and eight' as 1008. Rests on secure numerals to 100 and rote counting.
• Checkpoint — Tier A (age 6): count from 47 to 120 without error. Tier B (6–7): read the numeral 108 correctly. Tier C (7): write the numeral for 'one hundred and fifteen' (115), not 10015 or 1015.
bestPractices: Practise counting on FROM ANY number (start at 47, at 96, at 112) so children internalise that the count sequence can be entered anywhere — not a fixed chant from 1.
Give special attention to the 99→100 and 109→110 crossings and the 100–120 numerals, where the new hundreds place trips reading/writing.
Confront the write-what-you-hear trap for three-digit words: 'one hundred and eight' → 108, NOT 1008; use place-value/arrow cards (100 + 8) to show the zero tens placeholder.
Extend the 100-square to a 120-grid so the pattern continues visibly past 100 and children see 101–120 as 'one hundred and ...'.
Balance count / read / write and forwards/backwards across the boundary to build robust fluency.
keyRepresentations: Bead string / number line to 120 for counting on from any point and crossing 100.
Place-value / arrow cards composing 108 as 100 + 8 (zero-tens placeholder visible).
Number track segments across the 99→100 and 109→110 crossings.
commonMisconceptions: Writing three-digit words literally: 'one hundred and eight' → 1008, or 'one hundred and fifteen' → 10015/1015 (missing the zero-tens placeholder or concatenating).
Stalling or resetting at 100 (saying 'one hundred, two hundred' or restarting at 1) when counting on.
Only being able to count from 1, not from an arbitrary start number.
Reading 108 as 'ten eight' or 'one-oh-eight' without the hundred meaning.

learn.summary: For ages 6–7: count to 120 starting from ANY number below 120, and read/write numerals to 120. Two skills carry the load: (i) counting on from an arbitrary start (not always from 1), so children feel the count as a movable sequence they can enter anywhere; and (ii) crossing 100 — reading and writing 100–120, where the hundreds place appears and children must learn that 'one hundred and eight' is 108, not 1008. Give special attention to the 99→100 and 109→110 crossings and to the write-what-you-hear trap. The primary approach is an interactive 120-grid twinned with a number line; a static grid and short written/spoken checks are useful supporting tools with their own limits.

activities.title: Count on from any number across 100 (interactive grid and line)
feedback: If the count breaks at 99→100 or 109→110, don't reteach the whole sequence — rehearse just that boundary on a short track around it: 99, 100, 101 and 108, 109, 110.
If the child restarts at 1 or stalls at 100, nudge exactly at the boundary and model continuing: 'ninety-nine, one hundred, one hundred and one'.
If the child says 'nine hundred' after 99 or jumps to 200, point back to the grid so the next cell is visibly 100, then 101.
activities.rationale: Counting on from any number and crossing 100 are the known difficulty points for this age; rehearsing the exact boundary where errors cluster, with the sequence advancing visibly, is intended to build robust fluency. An interactive grid/line lets the child count, see the sequence advance, and get feedback at the boundary; a highlight-as-you-go display and a count-back mode make the mechanism concrete without being required.
sourceClaims: Grade 1 pupils count to 120 starting at any number less than 120, and read and write numerals in this range.
Year 1 pupils count to and across 100, forwards and backwards, beginning with 0 or 1 or from any given number.
Counting on from any number (not just from 1) and crossing the 100 boundary are known difficulty points; three-digit number words invite literal 'one hundred and eight = 1008' writing errors.
learnerActions: Pick any starting number — for example 47, 96, or 112 — and count on out loud, one number at a time, as each number is highlighted in turn on a 120-grid and a matching number line.

Deliberately practise starts that sit just before a boundary (start at 96 and count 97, 98, 99, 100, 101; start at 108 and count 109, 110, 111) so the century and decade rollovers get extra rehearsal.
Count backwards too (for example from 112 down past 100) to show the sequence runs both ways across the boundary.
While counting, keep the single running count going — avoid resetting to 1 or jumping to 'two hundred' after 100.
activities.intendedInsight: The count is a movable window you can enter at any number, not a fixed chant that must start at 1; it continues smoothly past 100, where 101–120 are 'one hundred and ...'.

activities.title: Build the numeral from the spoken words with place-value cards
feedback: If the child writes 1008 for 108 or 10015 for one hundred and fifteen, build the number with a hundred, tens and ones and write it into a hundreds/tens/ones frame; the 0 in 108 marks the empty tens.
If the child reads 108 as 'ten eight' or 'one-oh-eight' without the hundred meaning, point to the hundred card and reread 'one hundred and eight'.
When a written numeral like 1008 is 'too long', compare it to the 120-grid to show it would land far off the board.
activities.rationale: The literal 'write what you hear' error is a specific, documented misconception for three-digit words; making the zero-tens placeholder visible through arrow/place-value cards is intended to directly address how the numeral is composed. Rejecting 1008 by showing it lands off a 120-grid is an optional feedback device that makes the error visible, not a required mechanism.
sourceClaims: Counting on from any number (not just from 1) and crossing the 100 boundary are known difficulty points; three-digit number words invite literal 'one hundred and eight = 1008' writing errors.
Grade 1 pupils count to 120 starting at any number less than 120, and read and write numerals in this range.
learnerActions: Hear or read a number word such as 'one hundred and eight' and build it with place-value / arrow cards: pull the '100' card, note there are zero tens, then the '8' card, so the cards overlay to read 108.
Say what job the 0 is doing in 108 — it holds the empty tens place.
Do the same for 'one hundred and fifteen' → compose 100, then 1 ten, then 5, reading 115.
Confront the trap directly: write the words out literally (1008, 10015) and compare that number to where it would sit relative to the 120-grid — far off the board — to see why it can't be right.
activities.intendedInsight: Three-digit numerals are built by place value, not by stringing the spoken words together; the zero in 108 is a tens placeholder, and concatenating words gives numbers far too large.

activities.title: Fluency and trap checks: sequence, read, and write across 100
feedback: If a written answer is 1015 or 10015 for one hundred and fifteen, revisit the place-value build: 100, then 1 ten, then 5 → 115.
If a sequence answer breaks at 99→100, rehearse just that short run on a number line.
Confirm correct responses by rereading the numeral with its hundred meaning (108 = 'one hundred and eight').
activities.rationale: Short checks over sequence-filling, reading and words-to-numeral writing surface both the rollover stall and the concatenation error. These response formats are useful for checking fluency; note that choosing or completing an answer checks recognition and recall more than it elicits sustained independent counting, so pair it with the counting activity.
sourceClaims: Grade 1 pupils count to 120 starting at any number less than 120, and read and write numerals in this range.
Year 1 pupils count to and across 100, forwards and backwards, beginning with 0 or 1 or from any given number.
learnerActions: Fill the missing numbers in a run that crosses the boundary, e.g. 97, 98, __, __, 101.
Read a given numeral aloud, e.g. 108, as 'one hundred and eight'.
Write the numeral for a spoken/written number word, e.g. 'one hundred and fifteen' → 115.
Use a slider or marker to land on target numbers up to 120.
activities.intendedInsight: These checks show whether a learner can complete sequences across 100, read numerals 100–120 with their hundred meaning, and write them by place value rather than concatenating words; sustained counting across 100 is confirmed through the spoken counting activity.

activities.title: 120-grid as a reference map
feedback: If a child is unsure what follows 99 or 109, locate it on the grid and read the next cell.
Reinforce that the two rows above 100 repeat the pattern of the first two rows: 101–110 matches 1–10, and 111–120 matches 11–20, with 'one hundred and ...' in front.
activities.rationale: A static 120-grid is a valuable reference that makes the continuing pattern visible, which supports the extension past 100. On its own a fixed grid does not rehearse the productive skills of counting on and writing numerals, so use it alongside counting and composing activities rather than as the main vehicle.
learnerActions: Explore a 120-grid, tapping cells to hear and see each numeral, with 101–120 displayed as 'one hundred and ...'.
Trace the pattern down each column and across each row to see how the sequence continues past 100 just as it did below it.
Point to where 99, 100, 109 and 110 sit and name them.
activities.intendedInsight: The counting pattern continues unbroken past 100, and 101–120 keep the same ones/tens pattern with 'one hundred and ...' in front.

constraints: Rests on secure numerals to 100 and secure rote counting; if counting across 100 fails, check these prerequisites first.
Give deliberate extra practice at the 99→100 and 109→110 crossings and across 100–120, where reading/writing most often breaks.
A static 120-grid is a reference scaffold: it shows the pattern but does not itself let a child rehearse counting on or writing numerals, which are productive skills.
Choosing or completing answers checks recognition and recall; it does not by itself demonstrate sustained independent counting, so include spoken/written counting over a run that crosses 100.
Keep a single running count across the boundary — watch for resetting to 1, stalling at 100, or jumping to 'two hundred'.
Balance count / read / write and forwards/backwards across the boundary.
Checkpoints: count from 47 to 120 without error (age 6); read 108 correctly (6–7); write 115 for 'one hundred and fifteen', not 10015 or 1015 (age 7).
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

Two of the three cited sources (CCSS 1.NBT.1 and the NCETM guidance) are marked verified:false in the source row; the DfE National Curriculum claim is marked verified:true. Treat the unverified claims accordingly.

The legacy entry included universal-comparison boilerplate ('3D adds nothing', 'open dialogue adds little', 'a static picture can't rehearse') and fit rankings; these were removed or softened to scoped affordance/limit statements, since catalog ratings do not establish necessity or comparative efficacy.

Arithmetic/representation check: 108 = one hundred + zero tens + eight and 115 = one hundred + one ten + five are correct; the error targets 1008, 1015 and 10015 are correctly flagged as concatenation mistakes.

The static-grid reference activity's sourceClaims were set to [] because the available claims support the counting-across-100 topic rather than the specific principle that a static grid is a useful-but-limited reference.

Independent re-audit: no critical learner-facing errors, contradictions, or unsupported categorical medium claims remained; the previously flagged omission wording and the activity-4 sourceClaims were already corrected. sourceClaims in activities 1–3 cite claims whose specific skill content (count to 120 from any start, forwards/backwards across 100, read/write numerals) is directly exercised by those activities.

probeDeeper: What comes right after 99? And right after 109?
Write 108 — what job is the 0 doing?
assess.correctAnswer: Counts 97, 98, 99, 100, 101 … 110, 111 … without stalling; reads 108 as 'one hundred and eight'; writes 115.

errorPatterns.pattern: Stalls or resets at the century/decade rollover: after 99 goes back to a lower number, or after 109 is unsure what follows
errorPatterns.nextMove: Don't reteach the whole count — rehearse just the boundary on a 100–120 track/number line: 99, 100, 101 and 108, 109, 110.

errorPatterns.pattern: Concatenates the spoken words into digits: writes 1008 for 108 or 10015 for one hundred and fifteen
errorPatterns.nextMove: Build the number with a hundred, tens and ones and write it into a H/T/O frame; the 0 in 108 holds the empty tens.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Words-to-numeral produces a too-long number spelling out 'one hundred' + 'eight/fifteen'.

responseLevels.gap: Cannot count across 100 or writes concatenated numerals (1008, 10015).
responseLevels.full: Counts fluently from any start past 120 and reads/writes numerals to 120 including placeholder zeros.
responseLevels.partial: Counts and writes within the range but stalls at a rollover or drops/adds a placeholder digit.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Watch counting and writing across 100. 'Count on from 97 up past 110 for me. Read this: 108. Now write “one hundred and fifteen” as a numeral.' Watch the century rollover and the placeholder zero in 108.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: Crossing 99→100 and 109→110 is where the sequence breaks down; 108 and 115 both test whether the child builds the numeral by place value or concatenates the spoken words (1008, 10015). Watching the count in real time catches the stall.
